note: Pass rates recorded from eval runs while the retrieval pipeline was tuned. blind: the first time the set was scored against this code. tuned: failures from this set informed a change in this round or earlier.

rounds.change: First version of the lexicon and decision policy, before looking at any results.

Tuned on dev failures: field-weighted coverage, a clarification rule that requires the rival's title to cover the same query terms, capped weight for unknown words, action-only questions trigger clarification, two help-article fixes.

Wrote the second hold-out set, then tuned on test failures: 'number' means a phone number, stricter spelling correction (it turned 'connect' into 'contact'), definition questions route to the glossary, more filler words, four new article aliases, one reworded alias and one clearer article title.

Perspective-aware rewriting. The help centre is written by the vendor, so 'client' in an article means the user's own account; in a question it means one of the user's customers (a contact), unless it is plainly about their own account ('our client profile'). Before this, a help centre written in the vendor's voice failed 13 of 24 client/contact questions, with the forbidden article offered or ranked first 9 times. Then wrote the perspective hold-out set and scored it once.

Tuned on one perspective hold-out failure: 'the phone number on our client profile' ranked the contact article first. A number on the user's own account or profile now means the client contact number.

The shipped help centre now uses the vendor's voice throughout: 'client' means the user's own business ('Settings > Client profile', 'your client name'), and article lines that only existed to steer users from one article to another were removed. The prompt now carries an <interpretation> block saying which 'client' the user meant, and the eval checks it. No retrieval rule changed. From here the articles are frozen; the eval flags any change to them.

From a user report: 'change mode to online' was answered with the deal stage article, because spelling correction turned 'mode' into 'move'. Words under five letters are no longer spell-corrected, which also stops 'dead' becoming 'lead'. Questions about the assistant itself that would be escalated now explain the answer modes instead. Added four dev cases. No hold-out or perspective result changed.

Grounding and prompt-injection defences. An input guard blocks obvious injection before retrieval or any model call; the system prompt treats the question as untrusted and forbids anything but Harbour CRM help; the question is escaped so it can't close its tag; the model gets no tools or web access; answers containing links are withheld. Added twelve dev cases, two of them ordinary questions that must not be blocked. No hold-out or perspective result changed.

Cursory pen test: 38 probes covering instruction overrides, fake system messages, prompt extraction, role play, jailbreak phrases, spaced, leetspeak, accented, French, Spanish and base64 obfuscation, harmful and off-topic asks, and XSS payloads. On the first run 7 of the 27 injections were blocked, 19 were escalated by retrieval, 1 got the assistant-settings reply, and none was answered. The guard now normalises obfuscation and covers those shapes, and blocks all 27. The built site also gained a content security policy whose only cross-site API calls are to the Anthropic API (Google Fonts aside), and the SDK is bundled instead of loaded from a CDN. No other result changed.

Hybrid retrieval. A small embedding model (all-MiniLM-L6-v2, run in the browser) now sits behind keyword search. A new blind hold-out of 36 paraphrases that avoid the articles' wording was written and committed before any of this code. Keyword search decides first. When it would hand off to support and the closest semantic match is at least 0.45 similar, the bot suggests up to three articles instead of answering, so a wrong semantic match costs a click, not a wrong answer. The 0.45 threshold was chosen on 15 new dev paraphrases. Strict pass rates are unchanged on every existing case; 12 of the 15 new dev paraphrases fail strictly. The useful rate (answerable questions answered correctly or offered the right article) rose from 20% to 70% on the 30 answerable hard hold-out questions, from 82% to 100% on the original hold-out, and from 74% to 90% across the 162 answerable cases.

Added an everyday-voice set: 48 rambling, non-expert and deliberately ambiguous questions written by a separate agent that saw only the articles, never the code. It was scored blind and is not tuned on. Keyword search alone passed 13 of 48 (mostly hand-offs and blocks that were correct) and answered only 2 of the 30 answerable questions (6.7%): it usually ranked the right article first, but extra words dragged coverage below the escalate threshold. Semantic suggestions raise the useful rate on those 30 to 76.7%. A separate model comparison, where Claude makes the answer/ask/escalate decision, passes 78 to 85% of the everyday voice questions (86 to 92% across all four held-out sets). The retrieval code did not change.

Vector index and the wider Harbour suite. Semantic search now reads an HNSW graph index built at build time instead of scanning every passage; on all 304 questions it gives the same top article, top three and outcome as the flat scan, and a benchmark shows it at 1.4 ms against 64 ms at 100,000 passages. 969 help articles for five sister products were added, with product routing, "also in" links and cross-product suggestions; 9 hand-offs became suggestions from another product. Every document now has a status (draft, public, internal or archived) and only public ones reach the assistant; 190 withheld documents share the vector index and none surfaced (265 of 304 questions would surface one without the filter). A new blind set of 64 suite questions, written by a separate agent, passed 32 on its first and only scoring. Record types are now written as proper nouns (Contact, Deal) in the articles and app; no outcome changed.

Signed in or visitor. 15 overview pages for visitors were added beside the task help. Visitors search only the overview pages; signed in, the task help is searched first and the overview pages answer only when it would hand off. Weighting the overview pages down in one shared index was measured first and dropped: it changed 21 of the original answers. A blended weight with each set scored separately was measured too: it turned 2 hold-out suggestions into confident wrong answers and gained one question, so it was not shipped either. 48 new questions, half signed in and half as a visitor, were written blind by a separate agent. First scoring: signed in 11 of 24, visitor 12 of 24. Two changes followed. Overview answers stopped replacing suggestions, prompted by a dev-set failure. Exact title or alias matches now count for more on the overview pages, prompted by the owner's own example ("how do I add a contact" as a visitor), which is also in this set, so the visitor score below counts as tuned. The original questions are unchanged.

Record lookups. Signed in, questions about the account's own data ("show me Priya's phone number", "open Deals worth more than 10k", "Contacts at Kestrel") are answered straight from the records by a small deterministic parser, after the input guard and before help search, with no model call; record data never goes into a prompt. Everything it doesn't recognise goes to the help assistant as before. How-to questions that name a record get an "Open" link to it, and the name is replaced by its record type for help search. 40 lookup questions were written blind by a separate agent that read only the seed data. First scoring: 29 of 40. The parser was then widened for phrasings the failures showed it missed ("can you give me", "where is X located", "what deals do we have with X", "who works at X"). Widening made a list for a Company the account doesn't have list every Deal, so such a list now says it couldn't match the name. An independent review then fixed curly apostrophes, a Contact named with their Company, and statements such as "Priya has a new phone number". The lookup score below counts as tuned. None of the 416 help, viewer and suite questions is answered as data. Replacing names with record types changed 2 of the original 304 outcomes, both from a hand-off to a suggestion: strict pass rates are unchanged, and the useful rate on the never-tuned hard hold-out rose from 70.0% to 73.3%.

knownIssues: Unknown but harmless words ('typo', 'wrong', 'keep', 'paying') lower coverage, so keyword search hands off questions it could have answered. Since round 9, semantic suggestions offer the right article for 5 of the 6 hold-out failures; the sixth is 'change an address', answered from the company article instead of clarified.

Lexical retrieval can't tell 'send an invoice to a contact' (unsupported) from 'where invoices are sent' (billing email). In Claude mode the model is told to escalate when the article doesn't answer the question, which is the intended second line of defence.
'Change an address' is ambiguous between a company's postal address and an email address, but the policy answers with the company article.
'We have a new office number' is answered with the company article, not the client contact number. Without 'our' or 'account', nothing marks the number as the user's own.

The input guard is pattern-based, so a determined attacker can phrase an injection it doesn't recognise. Such a question still has to pass retrieval's coverage threshold, and then faces a model with no tools, a prompt that treats the question as untrusted, a reply schema that only allows citations of the articles provided, and an output check that withholds uncited or linked answers.

Semantic similarity alone can't separate a right paraphrase from a near-miss: "import contacts" scores 0.78 against the export article, higher than many true matches. That is why semantic search only suggests and never answers. Suggestions are also shown for 20 of 49 out-of-scope questions, where the user then picks Contact support.

Long, conversational questions add words the help centre never uses, so keyword coverage falls and the policy escalates even when the right article ranks first. Semantic suggestions recover most of these as suggestions, and a model making the decision recovers most as answers, at a per-question cost.
afterHoldout: After the hold-out run, articles declared as look-alikes stopped being passed to the model as extra context, and the core-example check got stricter: the forbidden article must not be ranked first, offered, put in the prompt or cited. Pass rates didn't change.

knowledgeBaseChanges.change: Metadata only: every article gained status: public (document lifecycle: draft, public, internal or archived). No text changed.

House style requested by the owner: record types written as proper nouns (Contact, Company, Deal, Client) in titles, bodies and the app UI. Retrieval lowercases text and the embedding model is uncased; all 304 outcomes and citations are identical before and after.
